analysis.one_liner: Requires private insurance to cover telehealth visits on the same terms as in-person care.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2021 and sent to its Health Subcommittee days later, and no vote was ever held before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans and insurers to cover any medically necessary service by phone or video if they cover it in person, with the same copays, deductibles, and provider payment rates. It also barred plans from requiring patients to have a prior relationship with a provider before getting telehealth care, and let plans waive cost-sharing for COVID-19 diagnosis and treatment. It applied to plan years starting on or after January 1, 2022, and it covered mental health and substance use services explicitly.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who want or need care by phone or video — especially people in rural areas, people with mobility or transportation barriers, and people seeking mental health or addiction treatment. They would get telehealth visits covered on the same cost-sharing terms as office visits, and they could see a telehealth provider without first establishing a relationship with an in-network doctor. Providers delivering telehealth would be reimbursed at the same rate as in-person care, making it financially viable for them to keep offering it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients using telehealth and telehealth providers

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover any eligible service delivered by phone or video if they would cover the same service in person, with the same cost-sharing — so a telehealth visit costs the patient no more than going to the office.
Insurers must reimburse telehealth providers at in-person rates, removing the financial penalty that otherwise discourages doctors from offering remote care.
Plans cannot require a patient to have a prior relationship with a provider, so people could use telehealth without first making an in-person trip to establish one.
Mental health and substance use disorder services are explicitly included, and plans may waive cost-sharing for services diagnosing or treating COVID-19.
Plans cannot steer patients away from telehealth with incentives or penalties for choosing it.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and individuals who fund group plans, who would bear the cost of covering telehealth at in-person reimbursement rates and equal cost-sharing. Premiums could rise modestly; insurers also lose the ability to restrict telehealth networks or steer patients to cheaper channels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and group plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: Reimbursing phone and video visits at the same rate as in-person care raises costs for plans and premiums for everyone, even though a remote visit often takes the provider less time and involves no facility overhead.
Payment parity can encourage more visits billed at in-person rates, including for care that could be handled by a quick message or self-care — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

The bill sets no quality standards for which services must be delivered remotely beyond the provider's own judgment that the service is 'able to be safely and effectively furnished via a telecommunications system,' which leaves room for disagreement about what belongs on a screen.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient benefit is real and concrete: guaranteed coverage, equal cost-sharing, and open access to remote mental health care. The cost is higher premiums for plan sponsors and members, and some risk of overuse billed at in-person rates. On balance the bill traded a modest, diffuse premium cost for a specific, direct access benefit, but it was a narrow, two-cosponsor bill that never got the committee consideration where such tradeoffs could have been refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in July 2021, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dean Phillips introduced the Telehealth Coverage and Payment Parity Act in the House on July 16, 2021, joined by Rep. Steve Chabot as cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee that writes health insurance requirements.
On July 19, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it sat with no further action.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers come out ahead: they never had to cover telehealth at in-person rates or open their networks to remote providers, and telehealth's mandatory payment parity never became permanent law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers avoided the telehealth mandate

for.name: Rep. Dean Phillips
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 16, 2021 and sought cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Steve Chabot
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health insurance law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee on July 19, 2021 and never scheduled a markup or committee vote on it.

against.name: House Speaker and majority leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor calendar in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote, as it never cleared committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but with only two cosponsors total it drew too little support in either party to reach a vote; the obstruction was procedural inaction by the Democratic-run committee rather than a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to cover telehealth at in-person reimbursement rates, apply equal cost-sharing, and stop restricting telehealth networks — removing their ability to steer patients away from remote care or pay less for it. Because it never became law, insurers avoided a new mandate.

Payment parity and a ban on prior-relationship requirements would have guaranteed telehealth companies in-person reimbursement rates and direct access to insured patients, locking in their channel as a permanent, paid part of private coverage. Their gain would have come alongside better patient access.
Employers funding group coverage would bear much of the cost of expanded, equally reimbursed telehealth benefits through higher premiums, while their employees gained access.
